title: Boundary checks
summary: Three distinctions from the BSCP notes: who may read a response, what a session proves, and which control stops injected script.

questions.prompt: A script on another site can read an authenticated response from yours. What went wrong?
choices: The browser refused to send the request
The server told the browser that the other origin may read the response
The session cookie was marked Secure
questions.explain: Cross-origin resource sharing decides whether foreign script may read the response. The request can still be sent. Cross-site request forgery is about an action caused by a request the browser attaches cookies to, not about reading the body.

questions.prompt: Someone is signed in and can open another person's record by changing an identifier. Where is the gap?
choices: Access control on that specific object
The absence of a login page
questions.explain: Authentication already established who they are. The missing check is whether that identity may use that object. That check is access control.

questions.prompt: Untrusted data is written into a page and the browser treats it as script. Which statement matches the notes?
choices: A content security policy is the fix, and encoding is optional
Encode for the context the data is written into. A tight content security policy is a second layer
Hiding the element with CSS contains it
Turning off cookies removes the issue
questions.explain: Output encoding stops the browser from treating data as script. A content security policy can limit what still runs if encoding fails. A policy that allows inline script does not contain the issue.
